channel.title: Daily Recap — 🔬 AI Research
channel.description: What happened in 🔬 AI Research, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: Jensen Huang resigns after 33 years leading Nvidia; Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO
item.description:
Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia and left its board, ending a 33-year run at the helm of the company he co-founded and turned into the most valuable chipmaker in the world. Colette Kress, formerly CFO, takes over as interim CEO.

The resignation is the biggest leadership shock in the AI industry this year, and the immediate question is what it means for American AI leadership and the open-source ecosystem that has grown up around Nvidia's hardware. Coverage of the reasons behind the exit has varied widely — from personal conduct to the company's aggressive business practices — and the full picture is still emerging. For now, the transition itself is the story: the person most associated with the AI boom is out, and Nvidia's next chapter starts without him.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Jensen Huang resigns after 33 years leading NVIDIA
  • The Zvi: Jensen Huang Resigns After Having Another Affair In Addition to the Chinese Spy

item.title: llama.cpp hits 1.0.0, a milestone for local AI
item.description:
llama.cpp, the open-source inference engine that powers much of the local AI ecosystem, has reached version 1.0.0. The release is framed as a stronger foundation for running models on consumer hardware — the project that lets developers and hobbyists run large language models on laptops and desktops rather than in the cloud.

A 1.0 release signals stability and a commitment to a dependable API, which matters for the dozens of tools and apps built on top of llama.cpp. For the local AI community, it is a marker that the ecosystem has matured from experimental to infrastructure — a base others can build on with confidence.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

item.title: AllenAI's XYBench tests whether models solve the problem behind the question
item.description:
The Allen Institute for AI has released XYBench, a new benchmark that evaluates whether AI models address the underlying problem behind a question, not just the question as literally asked. The idea targets a real gap in how models are measured: a model can answer the surface question correctly while missing what the user actually needs.

Benchmarks shape what labs optimize for, so a test that rewards understanding intent over literal compliance could push models toward more genuinely helpful behavior. It is a small release in a week dominated by industry news, but for researchers tracking evaluation, it is the kind of work that quietly changes what 'good' means.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

item.title: Nvidia's SimReady assets bring robot pick-and-place into simulation
item.description:
Nvidia and Hugging Face have published a walkthrough for building a robot pick-and-place simulation using SimReady assets — standardized, simulation-ready 3D models designed to behave realistically in virtual environments. The goal is to let robotics developers train and test manipulation tasks in simulation before ever touching physical hardware.

Simulation is where modern robotics development increasingly happens, because real-world robot time is expensive and slow. Standardized assets lower the barrier to entry: instead of building environments from scratch, developers can assemble a working pick-and-place setup and iterate on it quickly. It is a practical, developer-focused release rather than a research breakthrough — but it is exactly the kind of tooling that accelerates the field.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

item.title: Datasette ships two plugin updates for maps and tiles
item.description:
Simon Willison shipped updates to two of the oldest Datasette plugins. datasette-cluster-map 0.19 now works with Datasette 1.0a42 and depends on the new datasette-leaflet, while datasette-leaflet 0.3 fixes a referrer-policy issue: Datasette pages used a no-referrer header, which violated OpenStreetMap's policy that tile requests carry a referrer. The fix sets the referrer policy on tile requests themselves, passing the host but not the full page path.

It is a small, careful piece of open-source maintenance — the kind that keeps the mapping ecosystem working for everyone. The cluster-map release also shows off Datasette's redesigned facets with a map of power plants owned by California's PG&E.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: datasette-cluster-map 0.19
  • Simon Willison's Weblog: datasette-leaflet 0.3

item.title: ArtCraft cloned Photoshop with AI — and now wants to rebuild everything
item.description:
ArtCraft used AI to rewrite Photoshop as open-source software, and for CEO Brandon Thomas the vision is even bigger: to take back the internet. The project is a striking example of AI-assisted reimplementation — a small team using AI coding tools to recreate one of the most complex pieces of commercial software ever built.

If the approach scales, it raises uncomfortable questions for incumbent software giants: when a flagship product can be cloned in the open, the moat shifts from code to distribution, brand, and ecosystem. ArtCraft's ambition to "rebuild everything" is the latest signal that AI is turning software itself into a commodity that can be regenerated on demand.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"

item.title: Google enters the decision-model market
item.description:
November 11, 2026 was decision-models day: Google entered the decision model market, Cloudflare showed which parts of a build failure a classifier could handle, and TypeSafe AI showed off its production customers. Decision models — smaller, specialized models that classify, route, and decide rather than generate — are emerging as a distinct product category alongside chatbots and coding agents.

The entry of Google, plus real production use cases from Cloudflare and TypeSafe AI, suggests the field is moving from research curiosity to deployed infrastructure. For builders, the question is shifting from whether to use decision models to where they fit in the stack.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] D-Day (Decision Models Day)

item.title: The Jev revolution: what engineers are already building with System One models
item.description:
At the AI Engineer Code Summit, lead Jev creator Diogo Almeida called on developers to automate everything, and companies like Glean showed how they are already using Jev. System One models — fast, instinctive models in contrast to slower, deliberative reasoning models — are finding real production roles.

The summit demos suggest the frontier is no longer just about bigger reasoning models: the practical work is in pairing fast System One models with slower System Two reasoning, and in wiring both into automated workflows. Jev's momentum is a sign that the ecosystem is maturing around that split.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models

item.title: Gemini 4 pricing is confusing — Carbon and Argon cost the same, Hydrogen close behind
item.description:
Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today, the lowest-cost member of the Gemini 4 family — but the pricing is genuinely confusing. Hydrogen runs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 for output, which is not far off its much bigger siblings Carbon and Argon, both priced at $2.00 input and $10.00 output through November 30, rising to $4.00 and $20.00 from December 1.

Carbon and Argon are the same price as each other, and both are scheduled to double in December, which undercuts the usual logic of a model tiering scheme. Simon Willison's llm-gemini 0.37 release adds support for the new model, but the pricing structure itself remains hard to rationalize.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: llm-gemini 0.37

item.title: IBM's LLMON, an LLM-native markup language, lands in Granite 4.1
item.description:
IBM has introduced LLMON, an LLM-native markup language, now available in its Granite 4.1 models in 3B and 8B sizes. The idea is a markup format designed for language models rather than adapted from formats built for humans or browsers.

Smaller open models getting purpose-built tooling like this is a notable trend: rather than chasing the largest frontier models, IBM is betting that efficient, specialized models with native structured-output formats can win real enterprise workloads.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

item.title: Gemini Decision 1 joins the decision-model race — and copies Jev's homework
item.description:
Google has joined Jev and OpenAI in the decision-model category with Gemini Decision 1, and the new API is almost identical to Jev's: it supports the same three question types (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna decision model at 10 cents per million input tokens, with output free; Jev remains the cheapest of the three at 4.2 cents per million.

The differentiator is modality: Jev is text (and JSON) only, OpenAI handles text and images, while Gemini Decision 1 is fully multimodal, covering text, images, audio, and video. Decision models are fast becoming a distinct product category — cheap, specialized models for bulk judgment tasks — and Google's entry, with the broadest input support, raises the competitive bar for everyone.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Gemini Decisions API

item.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow reveals how Claude runs across four chip families
item.description:
Anthropic kicked off its IPO roadshow, and the roadshow video contains previously unreleased details about how the company operates — most notably a section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown, describing how Anthropic trains and serves Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

The multi-chip strategy is striking in an industry where most labs are effectively locked to one vendor's hardware. Running across all four major chip families gives Anthropic negotiating leverage, supply resilience, and cost flexibility — and it fits with the company's separate claim that its own models can now port Claude between chip architectures in days rather than months.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video

item.title: Claude Mythos 5.2 arrives — "the world's most powerful model"
item.description:
Anthropic has introduced Claude Mythos 5.2, billed as the world's most powerful model, alongside the Fable and Mythos 5.2 system card. The announcement is the latest step in the rapid frontier-model cadence, with each release raising the bar on capability — and on the safety documentation that accompanies it.

System cards have become the standard way labs disclose a model's training, evaluation results, and known risks, and the Mythos 5.2 card is the key document for anyone tracking where the frontier actually stands. Details in the source are brief, but the framing — a new most-powerful-model claim paired with a full system card — signals Anthropic positioning Mythos as its flagship as it heads into its IPO.

Sources

  • The Zvi: Fable and Mythos 5.2: The System Card

item.title: Mercor raises $750M Series D at a $20B valuation, $3B run rate
item.description:
Mercor, the AI data and talent company, has raised a $750 million Series D at a $20 billion valuation, with a $3 billion revenue run rate. The round is one of the largest of the year in the AI infrastructure space and puts Mercor among the most valuable private AI companies.

The numbers underline how central high-quality training data has become to the AI economy: the same data-broker market now under scrutiny for selling reinforcement-learning environments to Chinese labs is also generating run rates in the billions. Mercor's raise is a bet that demand for curated data and expert human input will keep growing as models get larger and more capable.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Mercor $750m Series D at $20B valuation, $3B run rate

item.title: AWS ships an official emulator — built by a swarm of agents
item.description:
AWS has finally released an official emulator for running tests against a local clone of its many services without provisioning a paid API key. The project itself is a showcase for agent-built software: it was written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents, producing 29,684 commits in the first three weeks. AWS's Swami Sivasubramanian described how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog.

For developers, the emulator fills a long-standing gap — local testing against AWS services has historically meant third-party tools or real cloud spend. It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows, and a single downloadable binary would make it far more useful as part of a standard test suite. Still, an official, agent-built emulator from AWS is a notable milestone for both cloud tooling and agentic coding at scale.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: aws-emulator

item.title: llm 0.37.2 fixes a flaw that could leak your OpenAI API key
item.description:
Simon Willison's llm tool has shipped version 0.37.2, fixing a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo. The tool's extra-openai-models.yaml mechanism lets users point llm at OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers — but two flaws could accidentally send a configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses-mode model was run with chat-completions output enabled.

The fix matters because llm is widely used to juggle multiple providers from one CLI, and an API key leaking to the wrong endpoint is exactly the kind of quiet, hard-to-notice failure that security tooling exists to catch. Users running OpenAI-compatible endpoints should update promptly.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: llm 0.37.2

item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon, hands-on: Google's best model yet — but the price doubles December 1
item.description:
Gemini 4 Carbon was announced two weeks ago for a subset of cyber defenders, but it's now available to everyone, and Simon Willison has put it through its paces via his llm-gemini 0.36 release. It's Google's best-ever Gemini, priced at launch at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output — comparable to GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5.

The catch is the price schedule: it doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st, putting it at Opus 5.5 levels. Willison also tested it with Google's Antigravity tooling and found the model's reasoning outputs strong. The launch pricing looks like a deliberate land-grab — try it cheap now, pay full price later.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: llm-gemini 0.36

item.title: Meta launches Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient model
item.description:
Meta has launched Muse Ember, its entry in the small-efficient-model category alongside Claude Haiku and GPT Luna. Meta describes it as its smallest and most efficient model, designed for complex reasoning execution and the repetitive work agents do all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.

For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 — $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output. For scale, today's other big release, Claude Fable 5.2, costs 80 times that at $8/$40. Ember is a bet that the agentic future needs cheap, fast workhorse models as much as it needs frontier giants.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember

item.title: Fable 5.2 retakes the #1 LLM spot — and responds to who owns the code
item.description:
Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 arrived on Anthropic's IPO roadshow day, with Fable retaking the world #1 LLM spot. But the more interesting detail is a prompting quirk Willison surfaced: Fable responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. When a prompt said nothing about ownership, or presented the codebase as someone else's, the model tended to add to the existing structure — even when that repeated existing code.

Tell it the codebase is its own, though, and it merges repeated code and improves structure as it works. It's a small but telling finding about how much these models infer from framing, and a practical tip for anyone using Fable on real code.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Fable 5.2 retakes World #1 LLM spot as $ANT IPO roadshow begins
  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2

item.title: OpenAI shows new ways of working with Codex at the AI Engineer Code Summit
item.description:
On the first day of the AI Engineer Code Summit, OpenAI showed how developers can steer Codex by voice, hand off work to the cloud, and make use of dots — its newer interface for orchestrating coding agents.

The direction is clear: coding agents are moving from a terminal you type into toward something you supervise — speaking instructions, delegating long-running tasks to the cloud, and managing multiple agents at once. The tooling is racing to keep up with how quickly developers are actually adopting this workflow.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: AI Engineer Code Summit: OpenAI on New Ways of Working With Codex

item.title: NaiveAI promises 2,100 tokens per second — and its coding holds up
item.description:
NaiveAI claims speeds that could top Artificial Analysis's speed rankings at 2,100 tokens per second. Latent.Space put it to a hands-on test, and the coding quality held up against DeepSeek — a strong result for a model whose main selling point is raw speed.

Speed has become a genuine axis of competition: for agentic coding loops, where a model may take dozens of steps, tokens per second translates directly into how fast you get an answer. If NaiveAI's numbers hold up in independent testing, it becomes a serious option for latency-sensitive coding work.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?

item.title: Designing for agents: inside Resend, where the docs are written for Claude Code
item.description:
Where does answer engine optimization end and agent experience begin? Latent.Space goes inside Resend with Zeno Rocha to look at how the company designs for AI agents: documentation written so Claude Code can pick the right email API, and tools built for agents to call directly.

It's an early look at a shift every API company will have to make — the audience for your docs and SDKs is increasingly not a human developer but an agent acting on their behalf. Resend's approach treats agent experience as a first-class design problem, not an afterthought.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend

item.title: A new lab asks what's missing from the AI debate
item.description:
AI as Normal Technology announced STABL — the Societal Transformation and AI Bottlenecks Lab — arguing that the public conversation about AI is missing a quadrant. The debate tends to split between techno-optimism and doom, or between capability hype and safety panic, while the slower, structural questions about how societies actually absorb new technology get neglected.

STABL aims to study exactly those bottlenecks: the institutional, economic, and social friction that determines whether AI's capabilities translate into real transformation. It's a useful frame — the history of general-purpose technologies suggests the bottlenecks, not the benchmarks, decide the pace of change.

Sources

  • AI as Normal Technology: The missing quadrant in responses to AI

item.title: Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 — and the "jagged AGI" debate ignites
item.description:
Anthropic released two new models today, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with Fable 5.2 immediately ranked first on Artificial Analysis. Anthropic says the model "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes" on its internal benchmarks, and Simon Willison has already added both models to his llm-anthropic plugin so they can be run from the command line.

Ethan Mollick, who had early access, put Fable 5.2 through a battery of hard tests and calls the result "almost AGI" — or what he terms "jagged AGI." In one shot it produced a video with a twist ending; it hacked a tiny USB keyboard into a working game console, drafted a plausible business by reading 201 local governments' public agendas, reconstructed W. H. Auden's famously grueling 1941 course, wrote a 182-page research paper, and built a site of more than 450 procedurally generated 3D worlds. But the jaggedness persists: it doesn't notice its own errors in taste or judgment, needed repeated steering to make things beautiful rather than merely correct, and at one point quietly built itself a bureaucracy of agent teams. Expert-level in most computer-based tasks, in other words — with gaps that are getting harder to describe.

Sources

  • Simon Willison: llm-anthropic 0.31
  • One Useful Thing: Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI

item.title: METR report: AI is now accelerating AI research twofold — and recursive self-improvement may be a year away
item.description:
METR has published an extensive report, based on unprecedented deep access to Anthropic's internal data, on how much AI is accelerating AI research — and therefore how close we may be to recursive self-improvement, where AI systems improve themselves. Its central finding: since October 2025, Anthropic's model capabilities have been advancing at roughly twice the rate they did from March 2024 to October 2025, with most of that acceleration probably attributable to AI doing AI R&D. A naive extrapolation puts full recursive self-improvement less than a year away, and METR found no observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns that would stop the acceleration.

The report is several months ahead of the AI 2027 timeline, and it has already pushed many forecasters toward shorter timelines. But there's a large caveat: Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence METR found most informative, so the public must largely take METR's judgment on trust. Zvi Mowshowitz, who reviewed the report, calls the situation grim but unsurprising — the labs' own insiders have been saying timelines are short — and notes the one escape hatch: "We could stop the labs. The labs could choose to stop."

Sources

  • The Zvi: AI R&D Is Accelerating Towards Potential RSI in 2027

item.title: The data lab feeding the frontier: Handshake AI went from launch to $1B in a year
item.description:
Latent.Space published its first deep dive into a data lab, profiling Handshake AI — a company that went from launch to a $1 billion valuation in one year by selling specialized data to frontier AI labs. The piece walks through specific examples of what the labs are actually buying, across finance, biology, and alignment work.

The story matters because data, not just compute, has become a central bottleneck and battleground in the frontier race. As models converge on similar architectures and training recipes, the differentiator increasingly lies in who can source, curate, and verify the highest-quality task data — and specialist labs like Handshake have turned that need into one of the fastest-growing businesses in AI. The deep dive is a window into a part of the AI supply chain that usually stays behind closed doors.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team

item.title: Import AI 480: self-sustaining space economies, AI for science, and Meta's perfect hands
item.description:
This week's Import AI newsletter leads with three threads. First, the prospect of self-sustaining space economies — and the question of when robots will be working on the Moon — as AI-driven automation meets the economics of off-world industry. Second, fresh evidence of AI accelerating scientific progress, a theme that dovetails with today's METR report on AI speeding up AI research itself.

Third, Meta is building what the newsletter calls "perfect hands for a superintelligence": robotic hands capable of the dexterity a future embodied AI would need. The through-line of the issue is that AI's frontier is no longer just better language models — it's the physical world, from lunar robots to robot hands, and the scientific process itself.

Sources

  • Import AI: Import AI 480: Self-sustaining space economies; AI for science progress, and Meta builds perfect hands for a superintelligence

item.title: HOPE: a smarter way to shrink giant mixture-of-experts models
item.description:
Researchers from Amazon have published HOPE — Higher-Order Pruning of Experts — a new method for shrinking mixture-of-experts language models, and the Hugging Face blog walks through how it works. MoE models like Qwen3.5-122B carry hundreds of experts per layer, and expert weights can take up 95% of the model's memory even though only a handful are used for any given token. Deleting the least useful experts is the obvious fix, but existing methods score each expert in isolation.

HOPE's insight is that experts don't work alone: they form stable cooperative groups that get co-activated together, so deleting one expert can break a partnership its neighbors rely on. By modeling pairwise interactions between experts and solving for the prune-set that minimizes the resulting error, HOPE preserves those clusters. At 50% pruning it beat every first-order baseline tested, and on Qwen3.5-35B it scored 42.3 on the agentic coding benchmark SWE-Bench Pro — matching the unpruned model's 41.8, where the best prior method dropped to 36.2. The team has released code to run the three-step calibrate–solve–prune pipeline on Qwen and GLM models.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

item.title: How Stanford teaches AI-native engineering when agents can do the homework
item.description:
What do you assign when a coding agent can finish last year's homework in one prompt? In the second run of Stanford's CS146S, instructor Mihail Eric brought open-source maintainers into the course. Students have to learn an unfamiliar repo, propose a change, and work with real maintainers — tasks that can't be one-shotted by an agent.

The course is a case study in how engineering education is adapting to AI: the value shifts from writing code from scratch to reading unfamiliar code, judging an agent's output, and collaborating with humans. Eric's approach — real repos, real stakeholders — is a template other programs are likely to copy.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
  • Latent.Space: [One Million AI Engineer Special] How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco

item.title: Hide your AI-written PR descriptions behind a details tag
item.description:
Simon Willison notes that most of his changes now arrive as PRs opened by Claude Code or Codex, and today's coding agents are almost too good at writing PR descriptions — accurate, comprehensive, and very long. The problem is that the detail buries the signal: reviewers have to wade through problem statements, solution details, and verification steps just to see what changed.

His fix is simple and practical: wrap the agent-written description in a collapsible details/summary block so the PR stays scannable while the full detail remains one click away. It's a small workflow habit for the age of AI-generated code, where the bottleneck is increasingly human attention, not output.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind

item.title: Building a SQLite parse_number() extension: C vs Rust, with Claude's help
item.description:
While walking the dog, Simon Willison got curious about writing a SQLite extension that adds a parse_number() function — turning strings like "-$1,234.56" or "12.5%" into numbers that can be summed and sorted. He fired up Claude (Opus 5.5) and asked it to explore the difference between building the extension in C versus Rust.

It's a window into how experienced developers now use AI: not to write the code directly, but as a research partner to compare implementation approaches before committing. The post walks through the trade-offs of each language for extension development, a niche but instructive comparison for anyone extending SQLite.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
